title: Decoupled Safety Control: A Safety-Control Algorithm for Training-Free Safety Guidance

paper.title: Decoupled Safety Control: A Safety-Control Algorithm for Training-Free Safety Guidance
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion models achieve strong performance in text-to-image generation, but they can still produce unsafe content. Training-free safety guidance offers a practical inference-time alternative that intervenes during sampling without modifying model weights. However, many existing safeguards still rely on a coupled safety-control chain. In this chain, the same unsafe condition simultaneously specifies what should be avoided, indicates the current unsafe signal, constructs the intervention, and determines when that intervention remains active. This coupling can work when unsafe factors are explicit, but becomes less reliable once harmful and benign semantics are entangled in the current generation state, often leaving residual unsafe content or unnecessarily degrading benign-generation quality or prompt fidelity. We address this problem with Decoupled Safety Control (DSC), a plug-in safety-control algorithm for training-free safety guidance. DSC reformulates training-free safety guidance as an explicit state-dependent control process, so the executed intervention is determined from the current generation state rather than inherited directly from a single unsafe condition. Experiments on standard safety benchmarks show that DSC improves representative latent- and text-space safeguards, achieving stronger unsafe-content suppression while preserving benign-generation quality and maintaining efficient inference.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models achieve strong performance in text-to-image generation [ Ho et al., 2020 , Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 , Karras et al., 2022 , Rombach et al., 2022 ] , but they also raise serious safety concerns. Open-source text-to-image models can still produce unsafe content and remain vulnerable to adversarial prompts [ Qu et al., 2023 , Tsai et al., 2024 , Zhang et al., 2024 , Chin et al., 2026 , Li et al., 2024a , Pham et al., 2023 , Yang et al., 2024a ] . Existing safety methods broadly fall into two groups. One line improves safety by fine-tuning or editing model weights [ Gandikota et al., 2023 , Gong et al., 2024 , Gandikota et al., 2024 , Kim et al., 2024 , Lu et al., 2024 , Li et al., 2024b , Srivatsan et al., 2025 ] . Although effective in many settings, these methods require additional optimization or direct parameter modification and can degrade benign generation quality. A complementary line instead performs training-free safety guidance during inference [ Schramowski et al., 2023 , Yoon et al., 2025 , Kim et al., 2026a , Kirchhof et al., 2025 , Kim et al., 2026b , Na et al., 2025 , Qiu et al., 2025 , Cao et al., 2025 , Zhang et al., 2025 ] . These methods preserve the base model parameters and can be used as plug-and-play safeguards. Among training-free safeguards, recent methods intervene at different sites in the denoising process. Early guidance-based methods such as Safe Latent Diffusion (SLD) [ Schramowski et al., 2023 ] modify classifier-free guidance with safety concepts or negative conditions [ Ho and Salimans, 2022 ] . Prompt-side methods such as Training-Free and Adaptive Guard for Safe Text-to-Image and Video Generation (SAFREE) [ Yoon et al., 2025 ] filter, project, or sanitize text representations against unsafe subspaces or directions [ Na et al., 2025 , Qiu et al., 2025 ] . More recent trajectory-level methods, including Safe Denoiser [ Kim et al., 2026a ] and Safety-Guided Flow (SGF) [ Kim et al., 2026b ] , alter the sampling trajectory using unsafe references, repulsive fields, or negative datasets [ Kirchhof et al., 2025 ] . Despite these differences, many safeguards still follow a similar safety-control chain organized around the same unsafe condition. In this safety-control chain, the same unsafe condition is often used to specify what should be avoided, indicate the current unsafe signal, construct the intervention, and determine when that intervention remains active. This coupled safety-control chain can be effective when unsafe factors are explicit and well aligned with the chosen unsafe condition. The limitation appears when harmful and benign semantics become entangled in the current generation state. In that case, the same unsafe condition is no longer sufficient to determine what should be preserved, which intervention is appropriate, or how long that intervention should remain active. Once harmful and benign semantics are entangled, the intervention becomes less reliable: it may suppress unsafe content too weakly and leave residual unsafe content, or suppress too broadly and degrade benign generation quality or prompt fidelity. This failure pattern is consistent with prior observations of quality degradation under hard filtering [ Yoon et al., 2025 ] , degraded performance on desired tasks [ Kim et al., 2026a ] , quality loss under prolonged negative guidance [ Kim et al., 2026b ] , and mode shift on complex prompts [ Li et al., 2025 ] . Taken together, these observations point to a common gap in current training-free safety guidance: the control process is not explicit enough to support a precise and reliable intervention. We address this gap with Decoupled Safety Control (DSC), a safety-control algorithm for training-free safety guidance. DSC makes the control process explicit through runtime evidence extraction, control-state estimation, intervention routing, update construction, and phase-aware execution. Intervention decisions depend on the current generation state rather than being inherited directly from a single unsafe condition. We instantiate DSC on representative latent- and text-space safeguards, including SLD and SAFREE, while keeping the base model unchanged. Experiments on standard safety benchmarks show that DSC achieves stronger unsafe-content suppression while preserving benign-generation quality, and remains efficient under the evaluated backbones. Our main contributions are as follows: • We identify a mechanism-level limitation in current training-free safety guidance: the same unsafe condition is often used to specify what should be avoided, indicate the current unsafe signal, construct the correction, and determine when the correction remains active. • We propose Decoupled Safety Control (DSC), a plug-in safety-control algorithm for training-free safety guidance that makes runtime evidence extraction, control-state estimation, intervention routing, update construction, and phase-aware execution explicit. • Experiments on standard safety benchmarks show that DSC improves representative latent- and text-space safeguards, achieving stronger unsafe-content suppression while preserving benign-generation quality and maintaining efficient inference under the evaluated backbones.

sections.heading: Training-based safety methods.
sections.text: Training-based safety methods improve safe generation by modifying model weights through concept erasure, model editing, or additional optimization. Representative parameter-level approaches include ESD [ Gandikota et al., 2023 ] , RECE [ Gong et al., 2024 ] , UCE [ Gandikota et al., 2024 ] , R.A.C.E. [ Kim et al., 2024 ] , MACE [ Lu et al., 2024 ] , machine unlearning for image-to-image generative models [ Li et al., 2024b ] , STEREO [ Srivatsan et al., 2025 ] , and Selective Amnesia [ Heng and Soh, 2023 ] . They can remove targeted unsafe concepts, but require retraining or direct parameter modification and may degrade benign generation quality. Our work instead focuses on inference-time safety control while keeping the base model unchanged.

sections.heading: Training-free latent- and prompt-space safeguards.
sections.text: Training-free safeguards instead intervene during inference without modifying model weights, either in latent space, as in Safe Latent Diffusion (SLD) [ Schramowski et al., 2023 ] , or in text/prompt space, as in Training-Free and Adaptive Guard for Safe Text-to-Image and Video Generation (SAFREE) [ Yoon et al., 2025 ] . SLD modifies classifier-free guidance with predefined safety prompts, while SAFREE filters unsafe prompt representations and adaptively reweights attention during sampling. Related variants include latent guarding, embedding guidance, prompt purification, and prompt-side steering [ Liu et al., 2024 , Na et al., 2025 , Qiu et al., 2025 , Qi et al., 2025 , Cao et al., 2025 , Zhang et al., 2025 ] . We focus on SLD and SAFREE as representative latent- and text-space safeguards whose interventions remain derived from pre-specified unsafe concepts, subspaces, or references.

sections.heading: Trajectory-level safety guidance.
sections.text: Trajectory-level safeguards directly modify the sampling path through unsafe references, repulsive fields, or time-varying negative guidance, as in Safe Denoiser [ Kim et al., 2026a ] , Shielded Diffusion [ Kirchhof et al., 2025 ] , and Safety-Guided Flow (SGF) [ Kim et al., 2026b ] . Related studies further analyze how negative prompts or negative guidance influence denoising behavior [ Ban et al., 2024 , Koulischer et al., 2025 , Li et al., 2025 ] . These methods address training-free safety by changing the denoising trajectory. Our work instead focuses on how the safety-control chain is organized once training-free intervention is introduced.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: We present Decoupled Safety Control (DSC), a plug-in control algorithm for training-free safety guidance. DSC makes the control process explicit at each denoising step. We first formulate the problem, then present Decoupled Safety Control, and finally describe its application to SLD and SAFREE. Figure 1: Overview of DSC at each denoising step. DSC organizes runtime evidence extraction, control-state estimation, intervention routing, update construction, and phase-aware execution around the baseline safeguard step.

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem Formulation
sections.text: Consider a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model with a training-free safeguard pipeline 𝒫 \mathcal{P} . Let x T ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) x_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) be the initial noise, and let x t x_{t} be the denoising state at step t t under prompt condition p p and safeguard condition c − c^{-} , where c − c^{-} denotes the unsafe concept, unsafe subspace, or unsafe reference set used by the safeguard. We write one safeguarded denoising step as x t − 1 𝒫 = H t ​ ( x t , p , c − , 𝒫 ) , x_{t-1}^{\mathcal{P}}=H_{t}(x_{t},p,c^{-};\mathcal{P}), (1) where H t H_{t} denotes the update produced by the safeguard at step t t . The objective is to generate a final sample that suppresses unsafe content associated with c − c^{-} while preserving the benign semantics in p p that are unrelated to the unsafe factor. This objective becomes challenging when harmful and benign semantics are entangled in the current trajectory, since the safeguard must decide not only whether to intervene, but also what should be suppressed, what should be preserved, and how strongly the intervention should act at the current step. Accordingly, we formulate training-free safe generation as a state-dependent control problem. In this formulation, unsafe specification remains fixed through the safeguard condition, while runtime evidence, control state, intervention route, update construction, and execution timing should be resolved from the current generation state. At each denoising step, the method should therefore infer the current control demand from the generation state and produce an intervention that balances unsafe suppression and benign preservation.

sections.heading: 3.2 Decoupled Safety Control
sections.text: Decoupled Safety Control (DSC) reformulates each safeguarded denoising step as an explicit state-dependent control process. At step t t , DSC extracts runtime evidence from the current generation state, estimates route-wise control states, selects an intervention route, constructs a route-conditioned update, and executes that update in a phase-aware manner. The executed intervention is therefore determined from the current generation state rather than inherited directly from a single unsafe condition.

sections.heading: Runtime evidence extraction.
sections.text: The safeguard condition specifies what should be avoided, but it need not by itself provide the most informative runtime evidence for the current denoising step. DSC therefore begins by extracting runtime evidence e t = Φ t ​ ( x t , p , c − , 𝒫 ) , e_{t}=\Phi_{t}(x_{t},p,c^{-};\mathcal{P}), (2) from the current generation state. The evidence e t e_{t} is the control-relevant observation used for subsequent control decisions. Depending on the safeguard, it may be formed from denoising-branch discrepancies, prompt-side filtering cues, predicted clean-sample relations, or support patterns exposed at the current step.

sections.heading: Intervention routing.
sections.text: Once the route-wise control states are identified, the method still must decide which intervention mode is appropriate for the current step. DSC therefore selects an intervention route from ℛ = { r sup , r bal , r rel } , \mathcal{R}=\{r^{\mathrm{sup}},r^{\mathrm{bal}},r^{\mathrm{rel}}\}, (8) where r sup r^{\mathrm{sup}} denotes suppressive control, r bal r^{\mathrm{bal}} denotes balanced, preservation-aware control, and r rel r^{\mathrm{rel}} denotes release toward the baseline dynamics. Suppressive control applies a direct unsafe correction when the current evidence supports it. Preservation-aware control constrains the correction when unsafe evidence overlaps with benign prompt semantics. Release returns the step toward the baseline safeguard dynamics when additional correction is not reliable. DSC first forms the admissible route set 𝒜 t = { r ∈ ℛ ∖ { r rel } : κ t ( r ) ≥ τ κ , η t ( r ) ≤ τ η , ω t ( r ) ≥ τ ω } , \mathcal{A}_{t}=\left\{r\in\mathcal{R}\setminus\{r^{\mathrm{rel}}\}:\kappa_{t}(r)\geq\tau_{\kappa},\;\eta_{t}(r)\leq\tau_{\eta},\;\omega_{t}(r)\geq\tau_{\omega}\right\}, (9) where τ κ \tau_{\kappa} , τ η \tau_{\eta} , and τ ω \tau_{\omega} are admissibility thresholds. This set keeps routes that are compatible with benign preservation, have limited suppressive-preservation leakage, and are reliable on the current support scope. Among the admissible routes, DSC selects the one with the strongest unsafe pressure: r t = { arg ⁡ max r ∈ 𝒜 t ​ π t ​ ( r ) , 𝒜 t ≠ ∅ , r rel , 𝒜 t = ∅ . r_{t}=\begin{cases}\arg\max_{r\in\mathcal{A}_{t}}\pi_{t}(r),&\mathcal{A}_{t}\neq\emptyset,\\ r^{\mathrm{rel}},&\mathcal{A}_{t}=\emptyset.\end{cases} (10) This routing step separates the intervention mode from the unsafe specification itself: the same unsafe condition can lead to suppressive, preservation-aware, or release behavior depending on the current runtime evidence.

sections.heading: Update construction.
sections.text: The selected route specifies the admissible correction mode at the current step, but that mode still must be instantiated in the safeguard space. DSC therefore constructs a route-conditioned update u ~ t = U t ​ ( x t , e t , s t ​ ( r t ) , r t , 𝒫 ) , \tilde{u}_{t}=U_{t}(x_{t},e_{t},s_{t}(r_{t}),r_{t};\mathcal{P}), (11) for the current safeguard. This stage realizes the selected intervention mode as the concrete safeguard-specific correction used at step t t . Different routes can therefore lead to different corrections under the same unsafe specification. The correction is stronger when the selected route has high unsafe pressure and milder when the selected route has high preservation demand or stronger suppressive-preservation leakage.

sections.heading: 3.3 Applied to SLD and SAFREE
sections.text: The DSC formulation separates the control stages from the underlying safeguard implementation. Applying it to a specific training-free safeguard only requires specifying the runtime evidence interface and the safeguard-specific realization of the correction, while the control-stage decomposition remains unchanged.

sections.heading: Applied to SLD.
sections.text: When applied to SLD [ Schramowski et al., 2023 ] , DSC uses the prompt, unconditional, and safety-concept denoising branches as its runtime evidence source. We denote the resulting SLD evidence by e t SLD = ( Δ t txt , Δ t safe , m t , q t ) , e_{t}^{\mathrm{SLD}}=\big(\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{txt}},\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{safe}},m_{t},q_{t}\big), (15) where Δ t txt = d ⁡ ( ϵ t txt , ϵ t uncond ) , Δ t safe = d ⁡ ( ϵ t txt , ϵ t safe ) , m t = cos ⁡ ( ϵ t txt − ϵ t uncond , ϵ t txt − ϵ t safe ) , \Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{txt}}=d\!\left(\epsilon_{t}^{\mathrm{txt}},\epsilon_{t}^{\mathrm{uncond}}\right),\qquad\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{safe}}=d\!\left(\epsilon_{t}^{\mathrm{txt}},\epsilon_{t}^{\mathrm{safe}}\right),\qquad m_{t}=\cos\!\left(\epsilon_{t}^{\mathrm{txt}}-\epsilon_{t}^{\mathrm{uncond}},\,\epsilon_{t}^{\mathrm{txt}}-\epsilon_{t}^{\mathrm{safe}}\right), (16) summarize the prompt-related and safety-related branch discrepancies together with their relative alignment at step t t , and q t q_{t} summarizes the current support pattern; here d ⁡ ( a , b ) = a − b d(a,b)=a-b denotes the branch discrepancy in the denoising space. In this latent-space application, d t − d_{t}^{-} is obtained from the safety-concept branch discrepancy, while d t + d_{t}^{+} is obtained from the prompt-preserving denoising direction. For each route, the corresponding candidate latent correction defines the suppressive direction g t r g_{t}^{r} , and the prompt-preserving denoising direction defines h t r h_{t}^{r} . The route-wise quantities in Eqs. ( 6 )–( 7 ) are then computed in the latent denoising space. Once the route is selected, DSC realizes the corresponding correction as an SLD-specific latent update, u ~ t SLD = U t SLD ​ ( x t , e t SLD , s t ​ ( r t ) , r t ) . \tilde{u}_{t}^{\mathrm{SLD}}=U_{t}^{\mathrm{SLD}}\!\left(x_{t},e_{t}^{\mathrm{SLD}},s_{t}(r_{t}),r_{t}\right). (17) The update is then executed through the same phase-aware mechanism in Eq. ( 13 ). Under this instantiation, DSC does not replace the SLD safeguard condition. Instead, it makes explicit how current latent evidence determines the intervention mode, its safeguard-specific realization, and its release timing.

In this prompt-space application, d t − d_{t}^{-} is obtained from the denoising discrepancy induced by the unsafe prompt-side cue, while d t + d_{t}^{+} is obtained from the preservation direction induced by the filtered benign prompt representation. For each route, the corresponding SAFREE-specific correction defines g t r g_{t}^{r} , and the filtered benign prompt representation induces the preservation direction h t r h_{t}^{r} . The route-wise quantities in Eqs. ( 6 )–( 7 ) are then computed in the SAFREE denoising space. DSC realizes the selected route as the corresponding SAFREE-specific correction u ~ t SAFREE = U t SAFREE ​ ( x t , e t SAFREE , s t ​ ( r t ) , r t ) . \tilde{u}_{t}^{\mathrm{SAFREE}}=U_{t}^{\mathrm{SAFREE}}\!\left(x_{t},e_{t}^{\mathrm{SAFREE}},s_{t}(r_{t}),r_{t}\right). sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: In this section, we study safety in text-to-image models on tasks involving adversarial nudity prompts and multi-category inappropriate content. The nudity task evaluates how well safety methods prevent harmful outputs as attack difficulty increases. The multi-category task assesses safety across several unsafe categories under the same control algorithm. We use Stable Diffusion (SD) v1.4 [ Rombach et al., 2022 ] with the DDPM sampler [ Ho et al., 2020 ] . To evaluate safety, we follow previous studies and report Attack Success Rate (ASR), Toxic Rate (TR), and Inappropriate Probability (IP) [ Schramowski et al., 2023 , Yoon et al., 2025 , Schramowski et al., 2022 ] . ASR and TR are used for the nudity benchmarks, and IP is used for the multi-category evaluation. Besides safety-related metrics, we also report Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [ Heusel et al., 2018 ] and CLIP score [ Radford et al., 2021 ] to evaluate image quality and prompt alignment. For Table 1 , we follow the released SGF benchmark code and use the COCO-30K prompt set with FID and CLIP computed on the first 10K prompt-image pairs. Unless otherwise noted, all methods use identical benchmark assets and evaluation settings for consistency; Appendix B summarizes the prompt sources, evaluator settings, and implementation details. Appendix E reports confidence intervals and additional automatic and human evaluations.

sections.heading: 4.1 Safe Generation against Nudity Prompts
sections.text: We follow the evaluation protocol used in recent training-free safe-generation studies [ Yoon et al., 2025 , Kim et al., 2026a , Kim et al., 2026b ] . For safety evaluation, we use Ring-A-Bell [ Tsai et al., 2024 ] , UnlearnDiff [ Zhang et al., 2024 ] , and MMA-Diffusion [ Yang et al., 2024b ] . For benign generation, we evaluate on COCO [ Lin et al., 2015 ] . We compare training-based baselines, including ESD and RECE [ Gandikota et al., 2023 , Gong et al., 2024 ] , with representative training-free safeguards, including SLD [ Schramowski et al., 2023 ] and SAFREE [ Yoon et al., 2025 ] . For the same underlying safeguards, we use SGF as the main recent enhancement baseline and compare it with Decoupled Safety Control. sections.heading: 5 Conclusions
sections.text: In this work, we identify a mechanism-level limitation in training-free safety guidance: the safety-control chain is often too coupled. We propose Decoupled Safety Control (DSC), which makes training-free intervention an explicit state-dependent control process during sampling. Across representative latent- and text-space safeguards, DSC reduces unsafe generation while preserving benign-generation quality under the evaluated settings. These results show that organizing safety guidance around explicit runtime control can improve training-free safeguards without modifying the base model.

sections.heading: Appendix A Limitations and Broader Impacts
sections.text: Limitations. Decoupled Safety Control is an inference-time safeguard for text-to-image generation. As with other benchmarked safety methods, the empirical evaluation in this paper uses released prompt sets, with automatic safety evaluators supplemented by human annotation. These protocols provide a consistent basis for comparison, but they do not fully capture all deployment settings. The method should therefore be understood as a practical layer of safety control in text-to-image systems. Broader impacts. This work aims to improve inference-time safety control for text-to-image generation. A positive impact is that stronger training-free safeguards may reduce harmful image generation without retraining or editing the base model. This can support safer deployment and evaluation of open text-to-image systems. At the same time, responsible use still requires careful benchmark-aware evaluation and appropriate handling of prompts and generated assets. Because safety mechanisms may still be probed or circumvented in practice, they should be used with benchmark-aware evaluation and appropriate review in deployment-sensitive settings.

sections.heading: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.text: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The abstract and introduction state the mechanism-level claim and scope of the paper, including the evaluated representative latent- and text-space safeguards; see the Abstract and Section 1. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The appendix discusses the limitations of the work under “Limitations and Broader Impacts”. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. • The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. • The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not claim formal theorem-level theoretical results or provide separate proofs. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper and appendix specify the benchmark assets, checkpoints, evaluators, sampling settings, and experimental protocols used for the main reported results. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. • Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [No] Justification: A code or data release package is not included with this paper. Reproducibility is documented through the main paper and appendix. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. • Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark). • The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. • The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. • At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). • Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper and appendix specify the benchmark splits, metrics, samplers, inference settings, evaluators, and ablation protocols used in the reported experiments. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. • The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Appendix E.1 reports prompt-cluster bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for MMA-Diffusion ASR and paired differences relative to SGF. The intervals quantify variability across sampled prompts under the evaluated image set. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. • The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. • For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). • If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper reports the GPU device, memory, and wall-clock timing for the shared overhead protocol, and the appendix documents the inference settings used across the reported evaluations. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. • The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. • The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines ? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper includes a content warning and a broader-impact discussion. The supplementary evaluation describes the human image-annotation protocol. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. • If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics. • The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The appendix discusses the intended safety benefit and responsible-use considerations, including the need for benchmark-aware evaluation of safeguards. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. • If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. • Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. • The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. • The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. • If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The submission does not release a new model, dataset, or code package as part of the paper package. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. • Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. • Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China Abstract Diffusion models achieve strong performance in text-to-image generation, but they can still produce unsafe content. Training-free safety guidance offers a practical inference-time alternative that intervenes during sampling without modifying model weights. However, many existing safeguards still rely on a coupled safety-control chain. In this chain, the same unsafe condition simultaneously specifies what should be avoided, indicates the current unsafe signal, constructs the intervention, and determines when that intervention remains active. This coupling can work when unsafe factors are explicit, but becomes less reliable once harmful and benign semantics are entangled in the current generation state, often leaving residual unsafe content or unnecessarily degrading benign-generation quality or prompt fidelity. We address this problem with Decoupled Safety Control (DSC), a plug-in safety-control algorithm for training-free safety guidance. DSC reformulates training-free safety guidance as an explicit state-dependent control process, so the executed intervention is determined from the current generation state rather than inherited directly from a single unsafe condition. Experiments on standard safety benchmarks show that DSC improves representative latent- and text-space safeguards, achieving stronger unsafe-content suppression while preserving benign-generation quality and maintaining efficient inference. Warning: This paper contains disturbing content, including censored examples of nudity and sexually explicit text prompts, included only for research and evaluation purposes. 1 Introduction Diffusion models achieve strong performance in text-to-image generation [ Ho et al., 2020 , Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 , Karras et al., 2022 , Rombach et al., 2022 ] , but they also raise serious safety concerns. Open-source text-to-image models can still produce unsafe content and remain vulnerable to adversarial prompts [ Qu et al., 2023 , Tsai et al., 2024 , Zhang et al., 2024 , Chin et al., 2026 , Li et al., 2024a , Pham et al., 2023 , Yang et al., 2024a ] . Existing safety methods broadly fall into two groups. One line improves safety by fine-tuning or editing model weights [ Gandikota et al., 2023 , Gong et al., 2024 , Gandikota et al., 2024 , Kim et al., 2024 , Lu et al., 2024 , Li et al., 2024b , Srivatsan et al., 2025 ] . Although effective in many settings, these methods require additional optimization or direct parameter modification and can degrade benign generation quality. A complementary line instead performs training-free safety guidance during inference [ Schramowski et al., 2023 , Yoon et al., 2025 , Kim et al., 2026a , Kirchhof et al., 2025 , Kim et al., 2026b , Na et al., 2025 , Qiu et al., 2025 , Cao et al., 2025 , Zhang et al., 2025 ] . These methods preserve the base model parameters and can be used as plug-and-play safeguards. Among training-free safeguards, recent methods intervene at different sites in the denoising process. Early guidance-based methods such as Safe Latent Diffusion (SLD) [ Schramowski et al., 2023 ] modify classifier-free guidance with safety concepts or negative conditions [ Ho and Salimans, 2022 ] . Prompt-side methods such as Training-Free and Adaptive Guard for Safe Text-to-Image and Video Generation (SAFREE) [ Yoon et al., 2025 ] filter, project, or sanitize text representations against unsafe subspaces or directions [ Na et al., 2025 , Qiu et al., 2025 ] . More recent trajectory-level methods, including Safe Denoiser [ Kim et al., 2026a ] and Safety-Guided Flow (SGF) [ Kim et al., 2026b ] , alter the sampling trajectory using unsafe references, repulsive fields, or negative datasets [ Kirchhof et al., 2025 ] . Despite these differences, many safeguards still follow a similar safety-control chain organized around the same unsafe condition. In this safety-control chain, the same unsafe condition is often used to specify what should be avoided, indicate the current unsafe signal, construct the intervention, and determine when that intervention remains active. This coupled safety-control chain can be effective when unsafe factors are explicit and well aligned with the chosen unsafe condition. The limitation appears when harmful and benign semantics become entangled in the current generation state. In that case, the same unsafe condition is no longer sufficient to determine what should be preserved, which intervention is appropriate, or how long that intervention should remain active. Once harmful and benign semantics are entangled, the intervention becomes less reliable: it may suppress unsafe content too weakly and leave residual unsafe content, or suppress too broadly and degrade benign generation quality or prompt fidelity. This failure pattern is consistent with prior observations of quality degradation under hard filtering [ Yoon et al., 2025 ] , degraded performance on desired tasks [ Kim et al., 2026a ] , quality loss under prolonged negative guidance [ Kim et al., 2026b ] , and mode shift on complex prompts [ Li et al., 2025 ] . Taken together, these observations point to a common gap in current training-free safety guidance: the control process is not explicit enough to support a precise and reliable intervention. We address this gap with Decoupled Safety Control (DSC), a safety-control algorithm for training-free safety guidance. DSC makes the control process explicit through runtime evidence extraction, control-state estimation, intervention routing, update construction, and phase-aware execution. Intervention decisions depend on the current generation state rather than being inherited directly from a single unsafe condition. We instantiate DSC on representative latent- and text-space safeguards, including SLD and SAFREE, while keeping the base model unchanged. Experiments on standard safety benchmarks show that DSC achieves stronger unsafe-content suppression while preserving benign-generation quality, and remains efficient under the evaluated backbones. Our main contributions are as follows: • We identify a mechanism-level limitation in current training-free safety guidance: the same unsafe condition is often used to specify what should be avoided, indicate the current unsafe signal, construct the correction, and determine when the correction remains active. • We propose Decoupled Safety Control (DSC), a plug-in safety-control algorithm for training-free safety guidance that makes runtime evidence extraction, control-state estimation, intervention routing, update construction, and phase-aware execution explicit. • Experiments on standard safety benchmarks show that DSC improves representative latent- and text-space safeguards, achieving stronger unsafe-content suppression while preserving benign-generation quality and maintaining efficient inference under the evaluated backbones. 2 Related Work Training-based safety methods. Training-based safety methods improve safe generation by modifying model weights through concept erasure, model editing, or additional optimization. Representative parameter-level approaches include ESD [ Gandikota et al., 2023 ] , RECE [ Gong et al., 2024 ] , UCE [ Gandikota et al., 2024 ] , R.A.C.E. [ Kim et al., 2024 ] , MACE [ Lu et al., 2024 ] , machine unlearning for image-to-image generative models [ Li et al., 2024b ] , STEREO [ Srivatsan et al., 2025 ] , and Selective Amnesia [ Heng and Soh, 2023 ] . They can remove targeted unsafe concepts, but require retraining or direct parameter modification and may degrade benign generation quality. Our work instead focuses on inference-time safety control while keeping the base model unchanged. Training-free latent- and prompt-space safeguards. Training-free safeguards instead intervene during inference without modifying model weights, either in latent space, as in Safe Latent Diffusion (SLD) [ Schramowski et al., 2023 ] , or in text/prompt space, as in Training-Free and Adaptive Guard for Safe Text-to-Image and Video Generation (SAFREE) [ Yoon et al., 2025 ] . SLD modifies classifier-free guidance with predefined safety prompts, while SAFREE filters unsafe prompt representations and adaptively reweights attention during sampling. Related variants include latent guarding, embedding guidance, prompt purification, and prompt-side steering [ Liu et al., 2024 , Na et al., 2025 , Qiu et al., 2025 , Qi et al., 2025 , Cao et al., 2025 , Zhang et al., 2025 ] . We focus on SLD and SAFREE as representative latent- and text-space safeguards whose interventions remain derived from pre-specified unsafe concepts, subspaces, or references. Trajectory-level safety guidance. Trajectory-level safeguards directly modify the sampling path through unsafe references, repulsive fields, or time-varying negative guidance, as in Safe Denoiser [ Kim et al., 2026a ] , Shielded Diffusion [ Kirchhof et al., 2025 ] , and Safety-Guided Flow (SGF) [ Kim et al., 2026b ] . Related studies further analyze how negative prompts or negative guidance influence denoising behavior [ Ban et al., 2024 , Koulischer et al., 2025 , Li et al., 2025 ] . These methods address training-free safety by changing the denoising trajectory. Our work instead focuses on how the safety-control chain is organized once training-free intervention is introduced. 3 Method We present Decoupled Safety Control (DSC), a plug-in control algorithm for training-free safety guidance. DSC makes the control process explicit at each denoising step. We first formulate the problem, then present Decoupled Safety Control, and finally describe its application to SLD and SAFREE. We propose Decoupled Safety Control (DSC), which makes training-free intervention an explicit state-dependent control process during sampling. Across representative latent- and text-space safeguards, DSC reduces unsafe generation while preserving benign-generation quality under the evaluated settings. These results show that organizing safety guidance around explicit runtime control can improve training-free safeguards without modifying the base model.
